We propose a flexible master’s program that offers an attractive path to an interdisciplinary graduate degree to current students in the URI online certificate programs and post-graduate professionals looking to bolster their skill sets and attain higher leadership positions and salaries.
The program would require students to successfully complete a graduate certificate program offered through URI Online, two elective courses, and four professional skills courses.
The mix of professional and discipline-specific skills and knowledge aims to prepare professionals for a broad range of careers across private industry, local, state, federal agencies, and community organizations.
Graduates of the program will be prepared to implement impactful societal, cultural, and economic initiatives.
The program speaks directly to the desire to foster a 21st-century, 24/7 learning environment.
Offered completely online and asynchronously, this program targets working professionals across various disciplines who wish to obtain their credentials while still holding full-time jobs.

The ‘a la carte’ nature of this program highlights the intersection of specialties employers are currently looking for while offering a flexible path to obtaining a master's degree.
Furthermore, the appeal of the in-state competitive tuition speaks to the accessibility of the program nationwide and beyond.
This program provides intellectual development for a diverse community of students.
The professional courses and graduate certificates push students to discover the synergies within their certificate areas and business/public administration to foster meaningful and impactful solutions and leadership.
The program integrates online certificate programs offered.
Students completing the certificates are accounted for within their respective programs, so it would not be considered an overlap but rather more of an inclusion.
This proposal describes a PSM framework under which focused tracks will be developed.
There are other master's degree programs that incorporate certificates into the masters (M aster's of Public Administration, M asters of Science in Healthcare M anagement, and proposed M asters of Science in Health Outcomes and Data Analytics).

They are very specific in their focus and audience.
For example, students entering the public administration realm will likely prefer an M PA over this program.
Similarly, students interested in applying data science to healthcare or focusing on healthcare management would likely choose those options.
This program allows for flexibility and broad appeal for students outside of those specific areas of focus.

Capstone projects will take one of the following forms, depending on availability in a given year: RITIN-affiliated or industry-sponsored projects, in which an external organization presents a real-world problem, and students analyze the issue and propose viable solutions (similar in structure to M BA capstone projects).
These projects will be sourced by graduate faculty advisors, with support from the College’s Professional and Executive Business Education (PEBE) team.
If such projects are not available in a given year, students will complete an industry-focused case study, such as a Harvard-style or Fashion Scholarship Fund (FSF)–inspired case, to be submitted to the department.

Remove comprehensive examinations associated with the two research methods courses in the program, and instead require comprehensive examinations in two elective TM D courses completed as part of the ABM degree.
These two courses will be aligned with the student’s area of specialization (i.e., Fashion M erchandising, Textile Science, or Fashion History and Conservation).
Rationale for the proposed restructuring of the ABM –TM D program To increase enrollment in the ABM –TM D program by offering a pathway that better aligns with undergraduate students’ career goals.
To better align the ABM –TM D curriculum with industry needs and expectations.
To provide students with practice-oriented, industry-relevant skills and experiences, rather than a primarily research-oriented academic experience.
Faculty observations indicate that undergraduate students who pursue the accelerated ABM –TM D pathway are primarily motivated by career preparation for the fashion and textile industry.
They seek advanced, applied skills and professional experiences that can directly support their transition into industry roles.

The current research-focused structure of the ABM –TM D program does not fully align with these career goals and, as a result, may limit the program’s appeal and effectiveness for this student population.After the first students went through the program, faculty were of the opinion that a higher threshold was needed for entry into a program designed to be completed in one year.

The current need for mental and behavioral health care in RI is well-documented (i.e., opiate and substance use crises, need for mental health services with emergent needs in child and adolescent mental health).
Furthermore, RI is designated as a Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA).
Therefore, there exists an urgent need for master’s level mental and behavioral health clinicians to meet workforce needs in RI and nationally to address these mental health and behavioral health needs.
The Department of Psychology currently has more than 1000 undergraduate majors whose bachelor’s degrees are not sufficient for entry into mental or behavioral health counseling positions.
Students who wish to work in delivery of mental and behavioral services require masters-level training that prepares them for state licensure.

The Psychology Department proposes to develop a professional non-thesis master’s degree in M ental and Behavioral Health Counseling at URI to help prepare committed applicants from psychology and related fields for employment opportunities in our field, helping to address the workforce needs of RI employers and, most importantly, supporting the development of these students into an essential resource to meet the critical mental and behavioral health needs of Rhode Islanders.
Graduates of this program will be eligible, with appropriate post-degree supervision hours, for licensure in the state of Rhode Island to become licensed mental health counselors (LM HCs).
These individuals can work in a range of settings (e.g., hospitals, private practice, community mental health centers) and, when licensed, provide services that can be reimbursed by all major insurance providers.
The Psychology Department has a 50-year history of applied graduate programs in Clinical (PhD) and historically School (master’s and PhD) focus areas.
Our PhD program in Clinical Psychology has been fully accredited by the American Psychological Association since 1972.

It is expected that a new professional M aster's degree program will easily fit into pre- existing resources and structures: 1) our existing graduate curriculum for our Clinical PhD program currently meets the Discipline-Specific Knowledge, Profession-Wide Competencies, and Learning/Curriculum Elements required by the American Psychological Association for M aster’s degree program accreditation, 2) faculty and staff are already teaching the majority of the required courses (didactic and experiential supervisory training), as well as 3) the Psychology Department has an in- house training clinic, the Psychological Consultation Center, that is directed by a full-time PhD clinical psychologist and is a principal training site for current doctoral students.
Psychology’s M aster’s Program in M ental and Behavioral Health Counseling proposed here aligns with several elements of the URI’s Strategic Plan including: 1.
Strategic Priority 1; Broadening URI’s Impact - Goal 1.

This program is designed to contribute to broad and deep impacts on the social, cultural, and economic ecosystems across Rhode Island, the nation and beyond – by increasing the number of M aster’s-trained license-eligible well prepared mental health professionals added to the RI and regional workforce to address pressing mental and behavioral health needs. 2.
Strategic Priority 2; Enhance Student Achievement- Goal 2: This new master’s program at URI will be a career preparation track that will be attractive to Psychology’s large pool of undergraduate majors as well as to regional applicants.
The significant need for well-trained license-eligible master’s students in RI, regionally, and nationally is likely to continue given mental illness upward trends. 3.

Strategic Priority 3; Foster an Inclusive Culture - Goal 2: This new master’s program will continue the Psychology Departments deep commitment to and significant ongoing efforts (e.g., standing departmental Inclusion and Diversity Committee) to build an innovative, contemporary, and professional learning environment and workplace that values diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility with leadership that is principle-centered and effective. 4.
Strategic Priority 4; Power the University of the Future - Goals 3 & 4: This new master’s program will help URI secure the necessary resources to sustain and grow the university and will generate a new revenue stream for years to come.

URI has the potential to be a major player in addressing our state’s mental health workforce needs as well as helping to address the national mental health crisis.
There would be modest overlap with the M aster of Science program in the Human Development and Family Science department insofar as both Programs would lead to licensure at the M aster's level.
However, the HDF program's graduates are eligible only to be licensed as M arriage and Family Therapists (LM FTs) whereas the graduates of the M asters in M ental and Behavioral Health Counseling will be eligible only to be licensed as M ental Health Counselors (LM HCs).
Although the two programs provide training in counseling and use external placements for their training, the two programs differ in terms of the requirements for licensure of the supervisors providing the training (students in the HDF M aster's require supervisors to be LM FTs; students in the M asters in M ental and Behavioral Health Counseling program will have supervisors who are LM HC, M SWs, or PhDs).

The two programs are working together to share resources to the benefit of both programs (e.g., students in each program will be required to take class(es) in the other program).
The M asters in M ental and Behavioral Health Counseling program will also overlap with the Clinical Psychology doctoral program; yet, we see this as tremendously advantageous to both programs.
M any courses in the Doctoral program will be shared with the M asters program ensuring fully enrolled classes that run each year (currently, several classes in the clinical program run every other year due to low enrollments).
In addition, the doctoral program has an excess of clinical externship sites requesting students for training.
The new M aster's program would help to meet this demand and offer training opportunities to students in placements that have long-standing training collaborations with the doctoral program.
Finally, the M asters program will offer courses (e.g., Group Counseling) that students in the doctoral program may wish to take.

Over the past five decades, demand for master’s degree programs in psychology has demonstrated strong and consistent yearly increases, evidencing a thriving field with strong growth potential (US Department of Education, 2022).
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, job growth in Substance Abuse, Behavioral Disorder, and M ental Health Counselors is expected to show 22% growth by 2031 (US Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2021).
Program graduates will meet the curricular requirements for licensure as a Licensed M ental Health Counselor in RI (and other states).
Licensed M ental Health Counselors in Rhode Island face a promising landscape of job opportunities, with high demand for counselors in various settings such as private practices, healthcare institutions, and community agencies.

Salaries for Licensed M ental Health Counselors in Rhode Island typically range from $65,000 to $110,000 annually, reflecting the importance placed on mental health and the valuable contributions these counselors make to the well-being of individuals and communities.

The monetary award of up to $2,000 supports students of promise to pursue research and/or practice in broadly defined areas relevant to child and adolescent psychology.
According to the US Bureau of Labor statistics, employment of mental health counselors is projected to grow the fastest among similar mental health occupations, increasing 22 percent from 2022 to 2032.

Regional competition includes a three-year Clinical Counseling Program with a specialization in either rehabilitation counseling or holistic mental health at Salve Regina University.
Roger Williams offers a Forensic M ental Health Counseling masters program geared to those wanting to provide services in forensic settings with populations including incarcerated individuals, those court-ordered to treatment, etc.
Both of these programs, however, offer education and training that is more specialized than the proposed M ental and Behavioral Health Counseling program.
Rhode Island College (RIC) offers a three-year M asters in Clinical M ental Health Counseling.
The program is accredited by the Council for Accreditation of Counseling and Related Educational Programs (CACREP).
The RIC program is also aimed at working professionals as the majority of their courses run in the evening.
The proposed M asters program at URI would be limited to 2-years plus an additional summer and considered a full-time program, with classes held in-person and typically during the day.
Additionally, we will be seeking accreditation from the American Psychological Association (not CACREP).

Johnson and Whales University offers an unaccredited 18-month masters in Clinical M ental Health Program.
We anticipate that the master’s program, when running at full capacity, will enroll approximately 20 students per year.
The program is expected to attract a large number of applicants, owing both to the size of our psychology major (currently the largest major in the University with over 1000 students) and the excellent reputation of our doctoral program in clinical psychology.
The Clinical Psychology doctoral program attracts 200-300 applicants each year and offers admission to fewer than 4% of all applicants.
We anticipate that a number of applicants who are unsuccessful in gaining entry into our doctoral program will choose to apply to the professional masters program.
Admission requirements include the following: personal statement addressing professional and research experience, interests, and goals; statement detailing how background and experiences demonstrate a commitment and ability to engage with issues of diversity and inclusion, three letters of reference, and a curriculum vita.
